html:
Jobs, waits and resume

A job is an action that takes time, such as a long command running in the background. SMTO keeps a record of the job so the assistant can follow it later. You do not need to keep the browser open, but the computer running the work and SMTO's main service must stay available for progress to continue.

A task can also wait for your answer, a tool result, a set time, or another event. SMTO saves what it is waiting for and continues the task when that condition is met. While waiting, it does not repeatedly ask the AI to make another decision.

Starting a job is not the same as finishing it. Check the completed result before relying on the answer. After an interruption, SMTO checks the saved job and the running program to find out whether work is still running, finished, or lost. If an action may have changed something but no result was received, it needs to be checked before being repeated. A cancellation stays tied to the job and task that were allowed to run.

Tool names for developers

These are the technical controls used by the assistant and integrations. You do not need to type them to follow a task in the activity history.

  • background=true starts a long command as a background job. Keep its job ID, which identifies that particular action.
  • inspect_execution reads saved progress and status without contacting the computer doing the work.
  • manage_job can check the computer for a fresh status, read a limited amount of output, cancel a job, check an unclear result, or wait for it.
  • wait_for_event saves a wait for a time, monitor, schedule, or trusted service event.

The implementation is in native/jobs.py and native/continuation.py. Saved results show what actually happened; a message saying a job started is not final output.

How work becomes eligible to resume

A job, an Activity and a native run have different lifetimes. The Gateway owns the process and its logs. The Controller retains job observations and execution receipts; Activities connect those facts to a task. The continuation worker decides whether a run may re-enter ordinary processing. Only the normal run and model-admission owners can authorize progression and inference.

flowchart TD Process[Gateway managed process and log stream] --> Observe[Shared Activity watchdog] Observe --> Facts[Correlated native job facts] Facts --> Settle[Job and Activity reconciliation] Settle --> Receipt[Exact result and completion mailbox] Settle --> Claims[Resource scheduler settlement] Claims --> Proof{Physical release established?} Proof -->|Yes| Capacity[Wake affected capacity waiters] Proof -->|No| Hold[Retain ownership or reconciliation prerequisite] Receipt --> Ready[Indexed run readiness] Capacity --> Ready Timer[Due timer or resource deadline] --> Ready Input[Accepted input or control event] --> Ready Ready --> Worker[Bounded continuation worker] Worker --> Check[Stop, Pause, ownership and wait checks] Check -->|Eligible| Run[Normal request and run claim] Run --> Model[Model capacity and decision acceptance] Check -->|Not eligible| Retain[Keep the checkpoint and subscriptions]

In the application, memory_continuation.py coalesces notifications by run, maintains dependency indexes and translates wall-clock deadlines into process-local monotonic deadlines. The MemoryContinuationWorker dequeues bounded batches and reconciles individual runs outside those transactions. It does not repeatedly scan all saved history. The standalone implementation in continuation.py retains a candidate scan and a half-second wake loop. Both use the same wait and resume contracts.

Managed job, completion and model consumption

For eligible captured Shell work, automatic promotion changes who observes the existing job. It keeps the operation, job and process identities. The attached path performs a final fresh completion probe at its promotion boundary; missing or uncertain evidence cannot become an invented successful completion. Explicit background work enters background observation after its launch acknowledgement.

sequenceDiagram participant A as Activity execution participant G as Captured Gateway participant W as Shared watchdog participant S as Native store participant C as Continuation and job reconciliation participant R as Owned Agent turn A->>G: Start admitted managed operation G-->>A: Job acknowledgement with same operation identity A->>S: Retain launch and Activity state alt Attached command finishes before promotion A->>W: Request fenced fresh status W->>G: Read correlated job status G-->>W: Terminal execution facts W->>S: Publish observation A->>S: Settle this job and exact receipt else Explicit background or promotion is eligible A->>S: Save queued or running background projection A->>W: Activate background observation of same job loop Until terminal facts or control uncertainty W->>G: Status or scheduled physical inspection G-->>W: Lifecycle evidence or unavailable control W->>S: Apply fenced observation and notify after commit end C->>S: Reconcile retained job and exact receipt C->>S: Append idempotent Activity completion end Note over C,S: Reconciliation asks the resource owner to settle physical claims C->>R: Resume only if control, wait and capacity checks permit R->>S: Prepare bounded completion delivery before inference Note over R,S: Events arriving during inference stay pending for a later boundary R->>S: Accept decision and acknowledge its exact delivery together

jobs.py binds every control call to the job's captured target, validates reply identity and preserves newer terminal observations over stale replies. Terminal log capture is bounded by the retained stream; missing output cannot erase execution truth. The Activity watchdog shares observation fences with fresh manual inspection. A failed observation remains a control failure, never proof that the process stopped.

background.py projects results and requests physical resource settlement. The completion mailbox retains undelivered events. Preparing model context does not acknowledge them: acknowledgement belongs to the accepted decision transaction. A crash or rejected decision therefore cannot silently consume a result. See model decisions and capacity for that transaction boundary.

Registering and waking a durable timer

wait_for_event resolves delay_seconds once into wake_at; recovery retains that absolute deadline. Non-time event IDs must have appeared in the current run's real tool results. Merely knowing another task's identifier does not create a valid wait.

sequenceDiagram participant T as Accepted wait control participant J as jobs.wait_for_event participant S as Native RAM authority participant I as Readiness indexes participant W as Continuation worker participant R as Normal run owner T->>J: Time delay or absolute wake_at J->>J: Validate, resolve once and advance wait generation J->>S: Save pending wait and continuation context S->>I: Refresh monotonic deadline for this run W->>I: Wait for relevant revision or next eligible deadline I-->>W: Deadline is due W->>S: Atomically take bounded ready work S->>S: Retain matching timer-expiration fact S-->>W: Run identity and readiness generation W->>W: Reconcile and recheck control, ownership and capacity alt Eligible now W->>R: Invoke normal resume callback R->>S: Claim progression and revalidate saved wait R->>S: Save wake, clear wait and discharge matching temporal requirement else Paused, stopping, owned or capacity-blocked W->>S: Preserve control state or register affected dependency end

A retained expiration remains true after a wall-clock rollback. Startup rebuilds monotonic indexes once from retained state; it does not add the original delay again. The callback still checks cancellation and deletion, then enters the normal request path. Neither a timer expiration nor its notification completes the user's deferred task.

Continuation arbitration

The following shows the application RAM worker's decision order. Reconciliation may update execution truth for paused or terminal tasks without resuming them. Controller admission and model endpoint admission are separate checks. A pending runtime-guard update or Pause request can require processing a budget-paused run; ordinary budget exhaustion alone does not resume it.

flowchart TD Take[Take one affected run] --> Exists{Retained and not tombstoned?} Exists -->|No| End[End this continuation attempt] Exists -->|Yes| Stop{Committed Stop?} Stop -->|Yes| Cancel[Advance cancellation or summary owner] Cancel --> ObserveStopped[Reconcile unfinished work when unowned] ObserveStopped --> End Stop -->|No| Owner{Progression already owned?} Owner -->|Yes| End Owner -->|No| Reconcile[Reconcile unfinished job and resource facts] Reconcile --> Controls{Paused, budget-blocked or nonrunnable?} Controls -->|Yes| End Controls -->|No| Pause{Pending Pause settles now?} Pause -->|Yes| Retain[Save paused checkpoint] Retain --> End Pause -->|No| Wake{Running or useful saved wake?} Wake -->|No| End Wake -->|Yes| Recheck{Still retained, unowned and not stopped?} Recheck -->|No| End Recheck -->|Yes| Admission{Controller can resume?} Admission -->|No| Subscribe[Watch capacity revision without losing a racing release] Subscribe --> End Admission -->|Yes| Callback[Normal resume callback acquires run authority] Callback --> Wait[Owned wait revalidation and evidence consumption] Wait --> Decision[Ordinary model decision path if still running]

A human checkpoint outranks a machine completion. wait_ready also recognizes accepted Activity input, permission changes, user amendments, result availability, selected job output/completion, monitor/schedule state and actionable supervision attention. A job output wake means more bytes exist beyond the saved cursor; it neither consumes those bytes nor implies process exit. Multi-job waits retain each identity and absolute cursor and return all currently ready selected jobs.

The worker observes capacity revisions before registering a blocked dependency. If capacity changes during that check, it queues the run again instead of losing the notification. An event arriving while a run owns progression is deferred until owner release. These are scheduling safeguards, not extra permission grants.

Resuming an Activity that needed input

A human answer, an OAuth completion and an unsafe-action approval have different consumers. All must correlate with the retained Activity and attempt. Independent background jobs can keep running while the parent displays one human checkpoint.

sequenceDiagram participant U as Accepted input or authorization owner participant S as Native store participant B as background.resume_inputs participant X as Existing retained executor or new claimed operation U->>S: Publish correlated Activity input event B->>S: Read unconsumed input under resumed run ownership B->>B: Check Pause, Stop, Activity state and operation identity alt Ordinary answer B->>B: Apply answer to its resource and append user context once B->>S: Save consumed event and completed input Activity else OAuth or approval B->>B: Retain previous attempt and bind original target context B->>S: Save consumption and continuation intent before execution alt Existing unsafe-action or HTTP continuation B->>X: Re-enter retained executor through retained admission else Ordinary approved retry B->>S: Save fresh operation and receipt identities B->>X: Recheck admission and claim exactly once end X-->>B: Actual receipt, another input wait or uncertain outcome B->>S: Save projection and eligible completion update end B->>B: Select next unanswered checkpoint or clear resolved parent wait

An ordinary answer completes the input checkpoint; it does not replay a business effect. An approved retry preserves the earlier receipt and uses the appropriate retained executor or a new physical operation identity. After interruption, a claimed attempt with no receipt remains uncertain. A repeated authorization event cannot by itself justify repeating that effect.

Recovery preserves execution identity

flowchart TD Restart[Recover interrupted active Activity] --> Job{Activity has a managed job?} Job -->|Yes| Observe[Observe same captured job and process identity] Observe --> Evidence{Correlated terminal evidence?} Evidence -->|Yes| Receipt[Settle exact result and Activity projection] Evidence -->|No| Live[Keep live or uncertain ownership and observation] Job -->|No| Foreground{Still owned by recovered foreground batch?} Foreground -->|Yes| Batch[Use Activity batch recovery rules] Foreground -->|No| Exact{Exact result exists for interrupted active attempt?} Exact -->|Yes| Result[Restore receipt-defined outcome] Exact -->|No| Unknown[Retain unknown outcome without relaunch] Receipt --> Physical[Resource owner evaluates physical release evidence] Result --> Physical Unknown --> Physical Physical -->|Unverified| Hold[Keep claim or reconciliation prerequisite] Physical -->|Verified| Release[Release ownership without rewriting outcome history] Batch --> Dispatch[See execution and receipt recovery]

Foreground claim repair inspects only the retained operation and target. A response for a different identity, an unreachable Gateway or a live process cannot establish release. The RAM worker retries orphaned claims with bounded per-run backoff. Clearing physical ownership never changes an unknown command into a successful one. See execution and receipt recovery and state and recovery for the related persistence boundaries.

Agent-controlled TTY commands

shell.command also accepts two explicit application modes:

Mode Backend Input
BatchModeTTY Managed terminal, like tty manage_job(action="input")
BatchModeNoTTY Managed process without a terminal Closed stdin; no subsequent input

Both return a job_id after launch acknowledgement without requiring background=true, including when automatic background execution is disabled. They retain existing job lifetime, detachment, cancellation, permission and recovery rules. TTY requires tty_jobs_v1; NoTTY requires background_jobs. Unsupported Gateways reject the request before launch. Both modes reject one-shot stdin; NoTTY also rejects interaction_mode="may_prompt". Existing execution modes and the captured default remain available.

These names do not change OpenSSH options. For password-capable SSH, use ssh -o BatchMode=no host 'command' with execution_mode="BatchModeTTY" and answer the login prompt through that job's input control. For unattended SSH, use ssh -o BatchMode=yes host 'command' with execution_mode="BatchModeNoTTY". Keep host-verification settings intact. OpenSSH's BatchMode=yes still prevents password prompting even inside a terminal. Failed commands are not automatically restarted in another mode. TTY retains ordinary prompt-based sudo; NoTTY retains managed non-TTY sudo and its remote-execution limitations. These modes do not add SSH working-context capture or credential storage.

shell.command(execution_mode="tty") starts one managed terminal per command and returns its job_id. It needs neither an open browser terminal nor background=true. Linux and macOS use a controlling POSIX terminal; Windows uses ConPTY when the required APIs are available (Windows 10 version 1809 / Windows Server 2019 onward). Gateways advertise support as tty_jobs_v1, also visible through gateway.scope and Shell discovery. Requests to older Gateways are rejected before execution.

The agent reads prompts through manage_job(action="logs") and answers the same process through manage_job(action="input", text=...). By default, input appends Enter unless the text already ends in a carriage return or newline. Send plain answers; an empty string presses Enter on its own. Backslash sequences remain literal data, so do not add textual \r or \n to an answer. Set submit=false for exact input, partial typing, or control keys such as Ctrl-C (JSON \u0003). The limit is 4,096 characters including the automatic Enter. One-shot stdin arguments cannot be combined with TTY mode. The controller prepares the final input before transport, so this also works with older TTY-capable Gateways.

shell.command(command="sudo id", execution_mode="tty")
manage_job(action="logs", job_id=<returned job>)
# If output requests a password:
manage_job(action="input", job_id=<same job>, text="<known password>")
# Observe subsequent output and eventual exit status.

TTY commands run unchanged, bypassing Gate sudo normalization and automatic elevation. The agent interprets prompts and supplies ordinary input. There are no password fields, prompt classifiers or password-specific UI in this feature. Existing command permissions and global logging/redaction settings still apply.

Logs combine terminal output using existing bounded storage and byte cursors. manage_job(action="wait", until="output", offset=<logs.next_offset>) waits for output beyond that cursor or process completion, including output that arrived before the wait was registered. A full log buffer is reported as truncated. Output waits support ordinary and TTY jobs. An explicit nonnegative integer offset is required; missing or invalid cursors are rejected before inspecting the job. Use the previous logs result's next_offset. Omitting until retains the existing completion wait. Activity shows output and process status through its existing surfaces.

For several endpoints, start one job per endpoint and use wait_for_any_job(jobs=[{"job_id": "...", "offset": 0}, ...], until="output"). Supply each offset from that job's previous logs.next_offset. The control accepts 1–64 distinct accessible jobs and returns every currently ready job with its identity, reason, status and references. It suspends inference when none is ready. Output, completion and unavailable/uncertain control state can resolve the wait. New output is not a password-prompt classification.

Read each ready job's logs, submit input only to the corresponding TTY job, remove finished jobs and wait again with updated cursors. Waiting does not consume output or advance cursors. Omit until and offsets to wait only for any completion or control uncertainty. Selection and absolute byte cursors survive controller recovery; evicted or purged output retains its normal reporting. This control neither launches jobs nor changes resource admission or concurrency limits.

The worker owns the terminal across browser/controller disconnects. Input uses the job's captured Gateway and owning run, and remains available while the command holds execution resources. Runtime delivery IDs prevent duplicate writes at the worker. An uncertain acknowledgement returns delivery_state="unknown"; inspect output/status before deciding what to do next, and never blindly resend. Recovery reconnects to a surviving worker without restarting the command. An exited job rejects further input; a missing worker reports input unavailable or uncertain.

Terminals start at 80 columns by 24 rows. Existing lifetime limits, cancellation and detachment controls apply. This interface has no reusable shell sessions, resize control or human terminal-input widget.

Detached managed jobs

Any command can use shell.command(background=true, detached=true) to run independently of task completion. An existing managed job can use manage_job(action="detach", job_id=...). This is explicit: ordinary background jobs still block completion, and requests to wait for results or monitor work retain the existing wait and monitor behavior.

Detachment keeps the captured Gateway owner, job ID, logs, resource claims and job_lifetime_seconds limit (zero means no lifetime cap). Normal task cleanup leaves detached processes running. They stop on their own exit, their lifetime deadline, or explicit cancellation. An explicit task Stop continues to cancel its owned jobs, including detached jobs. Detachment does not release resources or satisfy dependencies that require the command's result.

The agent can inspect or read logs, proceed with independent work, or finish. A confirmed running process supplies a separate launch reference proving only process start, never successful command completion. Queued or unknown execution supplies no such proof. manage_job(action="wait") also works on detached jobs when waiting is requested later. Detachment is durable across recovery; later observations cannot silently restore task ownership. Inspect, logs, wait and cancel continue to use the original scoped job handle.

Controller operation settlement

current_run/operation_settlement.py owns the shared deterministic release decision for synchronous operations, managed jobs and composite transfers. execution/lifecycle.py owns the producer contracts. The RAM and SQLite compatibility stores publish exact receipt/job evidence through this decision, in the same transaction as queue, lock, settlement event and affected activity updates. Existing lock hooks mirror queue transitions. Notifications occur after commit. A publication failure rolls everything back; duplicate evidence cannot reopen a released operation or replace an immutable receipt with conflicting evidence.

The live controller uses indexed RAM records and the existing hub commit. It does not connect to SQLite, scan disk, wait for a checkpoint, or scan retained ownership on every admission. Exact artifacts are inspected through immutable mappings; activity updates share unrelated output and history. Bootstrap checks retained ownership once before readiness. Owner reconciliation can also check a specific operation before making an authenticated Gateway inspection. SQLite remains an existing compatibility backend using the same release rules, not the RAM path.

The owned job record supersedes an earlier launch acknowledgement. Cross-run artifacts, inherited artifact links, model result projections, timestamps and local worker/PID exit cannot establish release. Derived receipts must explicitly supersede the original operation. Foreground inspection is bound by the existing owner to the retained target. Historical outcome uncertainty survives physical release, and late evidence preserves Stop and run ownership rather than resuming a cancelled task.

Namespace V2 binds concrete resources to captured execution domains; it does not change what proves physical end. An uncertain job retains its concrete resource claims while unrelated work may proceed within capacity limits. Host locks and historical global fallback fences are not part of the current locking model. Stopping the Controller or changing a display name cannot release or relabel an owned concrete claim. The authoritative scope rules are in resource scheduling. Retained input continuations require positive no-start evidence before reopening; the current run-owner lease consumes a single continuation generation while preserving the accepted profile. OAuth's _auth receipt is bound to that generation explicitly. Completed physical work stays fenced. The old no-start receipt cannot settle a later continuation. Its new completion must arrive through correlated source evidence.

Execution paths supply release proof at their own source boundary:

Path Release evidence Evidence that retains ownership
Synchronous tools, including filesystem and inspection tools The adapter's declared synchronous return An exception with possible execution or contradictory live-process facts
Shell/Python managed execution and background promotion The same operation's accepted job or foreground completion receipt Launch acknowledgement, live child, stale observation, or unknown process state
Independent completion, health and cancellation observers Correlated physical-end evidence settles job and closed sequence-parent claims in the observation transaction Missing supervisor, cancellation request, or unknown liveness; no run owner is required to publish valid release proof
Ordered shell.sequence Dispatcher closure plus exact same-run receipts/jobs for every claimed child Any missing, running, unbound or uncertain child; a still-open dispatcher
Activity/engine/child preflight rejection Source-owned proof that dispatch never started A replay or error returned after dispatch may have begun
Parallel batches and dependency graphs Each admitted child's own evidence Parent batch labels do not release child claims
Local controls The owning synchronous control return, when no external executor exists A business operation without execution evidence
Gateway transfer Explicit transfer completion and reconciliation evidence Lost commit acknowledgement or another unresolved transfer phase
Stop, failure and restart Confirmed execution inactivity, even if historical effects remain uncertain Task cancellation, worker exit or elapsed time alone

Shell sequence closure is committed with the invocation result and parent lock transition. The server verifies child operation identities, indexes and accepted commands; it does not use bounded child previews or a success label as execution proof. A failed or interrupted sequence can release once all attempted commands have ended. A child missing from a short error aggregate still counts if its invocation was claimed. Later child receipts and job observations settle a closed parent and wake waiting work in the same publication path. Approved retries validate reused prefix receipts without repeating commands. Bootstrap can repair older completed sequences from their retained invocation and child evidence.

The sequence-parent and preflight reservation fixes are server-side. Gateways still own physical command execution and its receipts. Resource release uses the concrete claims actually accepted for that operation.

Gateway selection is separate from physical resource identity. Each ordinary operation uses its captured pinned target; a transfer claims its source and destination paths. Optional physical-targets.json bootstrap evidence merges verified aliases of one physical machine. Without that evidence, pinned Gateways retain separate execution domains; they are not widened to external:*. Named HTTP origins and explicit shared resource keys can still conflict across targets. Opaque programs retain known concrete claims and disclose unresolved effects without a host or global fallback lock, so hidden effects require operator care when scheduling concurrent work. Changed trust prevents new admission but does not erase an already owned claim.

These rules come from execution_namespace.py, target_identity.py and the shared resource overlap vocabulary. A Gateway restart does not supply new Controller topology evidence.

A server restart invalidates its local progression and observation owners, then rebuilds resource ownership from retained execution evidence. It does not kill detached Gateway processes. Proven inactive jobs release during recovery or later observation; unknown jobs retain their reservations. In particular, supervisor_missing, executed=false and resource_claim_state=none do not establish inactivity when the Gateway still reports liveness_state=unknown. Restarting either service cannot manufacture a missing physical completion receipt. Completion observations settle physical claims without waiting for the old conversation to resume; semantic result delivery still uses the fenced completion mailbox.

A terminal outcome label does not retire observation while physical ownership remains unresolved. Recovery re-enables older prematurely retired observers. Cancellation and unknown jobs receive process inspection at bounded intervals even when optional health supervision is disabled; cached status alone cannot establish process death. Background recovery never changes an already released reservation back to active, including an explicit operator reset. Duplicate terminal publication preserves the accepted outcome and any newer physical release evidence on both storage backends.

The Gateway can establish that a detached worker never dispatched when its scoped IPC ticket identifies a dead worker, the durable dispatch fence is absent, and the job has no command identity or start evidence. The parent reaper also covers worker failure before PID binding. This closes the failed launch without replay. A legacy worker without a ticket, a live worker, a dispatch fence, or contradictory execution evidence remains unresolved. This launch recovery change requires the updated Gateway process as well as updated Controller observation code.

For a pre-lifecycle gateway.copy receipt, automatic compatibility repair requires an exact successful receipt plus its same-operation checkpoint: matching transfer identity, both Gateway/path pairs, verified phase, byte counts, SHA-256 verification and completed cleanup. A lost commit acknowledgement retains the claim until provider reconciliation proves its outcome. Successful destination publication can release while cleanup of isolated handles/staging remains pending; cleanup cannot subsequently publish the destination. Recovery never retransfers bytes.

Scheduling-profile observations expose a read-only settlement diagnostic, including release_pending when release proof exists but publication was lost. Status GETs never repair ownership. Lifecycle projection deduplicates foreground, batch history, dependency and background activities by execution identity, then uses current job/queue ownership. A lock wait remains distinct from capacity waiting and cannot be reported as all required work settled.

tests/test_operation_settlement.py exercises backend parity, rollback, unknown commit retention, supersession, stale observations, stopped runs, read-only diagnostics, no-SQL RAM admission and checkpoint recovery. Run python -m tests.benchmark_operation_settlement to measure RAM admission and receipt/settlement publication with retained history; it reports latency without using machine-load-sensitive correctness assertions. Settlement and projection make zero helper model calls.

tests/test_sequence_settlement.py adds closed-parent, late-child, malformed evidence, approved-prefix and checkpoint recovery cases. tests/test_resource_lock_execution_paths.py exercises complete dispatch and following-command admission on both backends, all three result delivery modes, preflight rejection, dispatcher exceptions and real subprocesses.

Gateway history intentionally coordinates physical resources across conversations. Effect classification and resource descriptors carry revisions and upgrade lazily without deleting jobs. Admission repairs stale classifications, recovers authoritative receipts, observes supported literal filesystem effects once per material revision, and checks structured resource overlap before rejecting new work. Opaque commands retain conservative ownership.

Abandoned claims are repaired automatically before admission or during correlated recovery inspection. If a job still owns the resource, the conversation offers waiting or forceful termination. The Gateway binds recovery to the rejected source operation and current blocker revision and keeps original receipts intact. Older saved baseline decisions remain readable for compatibility.

The runtime saves the exact never-executed candidate and continues it under one linked successor identity before another model decision. Existing permissions and Stop remain authoritative. A claimed successor with a missing receipt is inspected, never blindly replayed. Restart reconstructs the pending decision or accepted continuation from the same run store.

Foreground supervision and resource waits

The Gateway server PID identifies the controller hosting a foreground stream. It is not the lifetime of that command. Protocol 3 records supervision_kind, supervision_state, and the scope's start/end reason separately. Every completion receipt closes foreground supervision, including outcome_unknown. Stream loss closes supervision while retaining the actual command PID, creation time, group and session. A living child or descendant still holds ownership; a dead foreground tree releases physical ownership even while the Gateway server stays alive. Unobservable identity remains a reconciliation prerequisite. A known completion receipt is distinct from a successful outcome.

Older JSON job rows upgrade lazily during inspection/admission. A foreground row with a finish timestamp is interpreted as ended supervision. If its process tree is dead and both execution and possible effects are false, its stale claim releases and the original waiting candidate proceeds automatically. Unknown effects remain unknown in the audit when an abandoned claim is repaired. No job history is deleted. lost is an execution-control outcome, not proof of process-tree death; a surviving or unobservable tree still protects its resource.

Short resource waits emit an activity explaining that the command has not started. Admission saves correlated, allowlisted blocker facts and a progress timestamp. After 15 seconds without a material blocker change, a never-executed candidate enters the existing native resource decision. Unobservable ownership escalates after bounded reconciliation immediately. This interval requests attention; it never proves process death or expires an active claim.

Recovery appears inline in the conversation using the same disclosure and controls as Agent checks. It offers only Wait until the job state changes and Resolve forcefully by terminating job. Waiting persists across restarts until the claim resolves or the task is stopped/paused; it does not expire after 15 seconds and does not poll the model.

The Gateway automatically repairs abandoned claims with no recorded child identity or a verified dead process. Active supervision, unexpired launch leases, live process trees and inaccessible recorded identities prevent automatic repair. A small conversation notice records the repair. The old command outcome remains unknown; clearing ownership never fabricates success or replays the old command.

Forceful resolution records durable intent, kills the recorded process tree after checking its identity, verifies termination, and restores the saved claims. With no recorded child, an abandoned claim can be restored directly. Unknown effects and unverified termination remain in the audit. New process identities invalidate old resets; all decisions are correlated with the blocked operation and current claim revision. Repeated delivery and restart cannot duplicate a reset.

Reset remains available after Stop, which preserves the task's cancelled state. Active tasks continue the exact saved, never-executed invocation once through ordinary capability and permission checks. An unreceipted successor is inspected rather than relaunched. Browser presence has no execution authority.

Observation without execution

current_run/execution_observation.py is the shared controller-local read owner for the Agent's inspect_execution control and GET /api/agent/executions/{identity}/observation. It resolves retained request, run, task, Activity, operation and job identities. A conversation-only lookup requires an unambiguous current execution. Combined identities must correlate; tombstoned and foreign-conversation state is not observable. Arbitrary PID, path, hostname and command inputs are not execution observation identities.

The service reads selected native/job fields and Scheduler.observe diagnostics in query-only transactions. It never reaps, reconciles, repairs a claim, touches a target, creates an admission row or calls a model. The model control goes directly to this same service before target preflight and admission. Inspecting a held operation therefore does not queue behind that operation's resource slot. UI inspection can follow an owned blocking operation to its retained job facts without running a new Shell check.

Admission, process liveness, progress and outcome are separate facts. Pending admission means “Not started”; an acquired slot alone does not prove a process is alive. Only a recent correlated lifecycle-owner observation establishes liveness. Progress requires declared job-level counters. Output, CPU and I/O changes establish activity, not advancement of the task's declared work. A heartbeat is neither liveness nor progress. Missing contracts produce “Alive · progress unknown.” “Possibly stalled” requires a trusted progress contract, a known live process, at least three fresh comparable observations and the accepted inactivity threshold (90 seconds by default); it never fails or cancels the job. Receipt-defined terminal outcome overrides stale admission evidence.

Run terminal/checkpoint controls take precedence in the conversation. Below those, explicit dependency, effect and capacity waits take precedence over model narration. “Let me check” is an intention, never proof that a check started. Connection freshness is displayed separately and elapsed time comes from server timestamps. Existing recovery interactions and unknown-effect protections retain their execution authority.

Activity supervision

Managed inspectable jobs share one application-owned observation worker and a pool of four observers. Foreground Shell/Python operations with negotiated job support use the same operation identity; promotion does not start another watcher. Explicit external waits are excluded. Persistent services and opaque processes remain observable but silence alone never makes them stalled.

Completion detection and health supervision have separate clocks. Auto-managed Shell commands first remain attached to their original tool call. The runtime reads compact Gateway status every 250 ms, including a final fresh read at the promotion deadline. Short commands settle in that same Agent turn without promotion or supervision trace rows. Promotion transfers observation of the same job, PID, receipt lineage and claims; it never launches a replacement process. Python currently uses synchronous foreground execution and retains its direct receipt as completion authority.

Workspace-terminal routing negotiates workspace_shared_shells_v2 explicitly. gateway_core/shared_shell.py owns one persistent Bash 5+ PTY per Agent/Code tab. A private command-boundary pipe and acknowledgement barrier separate command start, output, exit status and cwd from terminal rendering. Human commands have their own Gateway job records and origin; they are never native agent tool executions. Every command releases its launch slot and resource reservation on its completion receipt, even though the shell remains alive. Idle typing owns the lane before submission. Shared launch and keyboard input use the same lock, and receipts bind input to the exact command or idle revision. Session loss never authorizes command replay.

Ordinary commands retain cwd and exports. Invocation metadata is scoped to the command. Explicit cwd, saved-copy execution, stdin, NoTTY and elevation retain their existing contracts; specialized command-owned workers occupy the same lane. Optional per-run /tmp mounts use the existing validated managed-TMPDIR fallback before shared-shell execution, since a persistent shell cannot switch mount namespaces for each run. Both Controller and Gateway must be updated before enabling this route; shared shells initialize only at an idle boundary.

Shared-shell agent invocations scope the same automatic-pager defaults as captured terminal commands to function-local exports. Explicit invocation environment values can override them, and the human shell's exports survive. This avoids automatic Git/less waits without removing interactive commands or terminal IO.

gateway_core/terminal_handoff.py watches recognized prompts, including pagers; silence alone never starts a countdown. Only agent-origin commands are eligible. workspace_terminal_input_timeout_seconds is a live, persisted Execution setting with a default of 10 positive whole seconds. Changes affect the next prompt. Each input request carries an identity, phase, revision, server time and deadline. Repeated status or output observations cannot restart the same request. Deadlines and typing pauses survive browser reconnects. Task Pause freezes the remaining countdown; Stop closes it. Toggle-off closes pending takeover immediately without restarting the running command.

Human typing invalidates outstanding model input at the physical writer and pauses handoff until submission. Pagers accept individual raw keys; raw readline editing retains human ownership. Let agent handle waits for buffered UI input and clears an unfinished line using the terminal's canonical kill character without submitting it. If a safe boundary is unavailable, it refuses handoff. Existing delivery IDs still deduplicate physical input. An expired countdown makes the request ready for the existing continuation owner; inference may take additional time.

The agent inspects live output and the current token, then uses manage_job input on the same job. manage_job request_input covers unrecognized prompts, while answer_needed retains the wait when task context lacks an answer or credential. Result subscriptions keep their concrete source jobs and survive an interruption for terminal attention. Re-registering a wait does not rearm a consumed prompt; a new prompt or explicit human trigger can wake it again. An attached launch that reaches handoff returns the input request and instructions to answer it.

A follow-up blocked by its own terminal receives an explicit no-start result identifying that job. Declared dependencies retain their queue position and can wake for a prompt in the exact blocking terminal. Handoff never releases resource ownership. Native tests cover both stores, real successive Git/less pagers and shared-shell receipts, capacity, cancellation and input races. Browser tests cover Agent/Code idle input, independent User shells, countdown, safe handoff, reload and settings persistence. Native Windows ConPTY retains its original execution flow.

After explicit background launch or promotion, the shared worker reads completion status every 500 ms for ten seconds, every second through sixty seconds, then every two seconds. Launch and cancellation confirmation use 250 ms. Status reads persisted lifecycle facts without process telemetry, log fetching, or PID-based outcome inference. Identical active status does not rewrite the native job. Completion probes produce no trace history or model calls. They remain active when health supervision is disabled.

The accepted activity_supervision_policy defaults to enabled. Background health is first inspected after 15 seconds, then every 25 seconds while healthy (30 seconds after 30 minutes). Unconfirmed starting states get a one-second health recheck independently of their faster completion clock. Quiet jobs are checked every 10 seconds. At least three fresh comparable observations and 90 seconds without declared progress are needed for “Possibly stalled”; attention starts at 180 seconds. A producer's progress_idle_threshold_seconds sets a minimum for both thresholds. The health inspection interval controls deeper supervision of already-running long work. It does not slow completion detection for normal commands. Timeout, cancellation and resource-claim owners retain their authority.

Automatic sustained_no_progress attention requires progress_expected=true and supported monotonic progress_metrics: bytes_transferred, items_completed, or steps_completed. These are trusted runtime/Gateway metadata, never model arguments, command-name guesses, or parsed log prose. CPU, I/O and output changes cannot conceal stagnant declared counters; their absence cannot establish a stall. Missing or invalid metrics, counter resets and changed identities establish a fresh baseline. Legacy Gateways and generic quiet Shell/Python processes remain progress-unknown. Gateway inspection samples outside its SQLite writer transaction and compares process identity again before publishing. A PID reuse or inaccessible sample cannot establish progress or process death.

Observation failures use a separate ten-second retry cadence and become attention-worthy after 90 seconds. They do not fail the job or release claims. Stop, newer progress and terminal truth suppress stale attention. Supervision never automatically kills work. Disabling supervision prevents health attention; ordinary completion probing remains active. The 30-second fallback only repairs legacy jobs missing a current observation record.

The indexed native_activity_watchdogs table retains one bounded latest record per Activity, with runtime-owned launch_pending, attached_completion, background_health, cancel_confirmation and terminal phases. Independent completion and health deadlines feed an indexed next_due_at. Claims make fresh manual and scheduled observations single-flight. Attached completion has reserved observation capacity. observation_capacity.py keeps separate process-local observation, completion and control lanes for each store path and RAM-hub epoch. Observation and completion each use the configured observation_slots limit (default four); control has its own single slot. These are remote-I/O reservations, separate from workload claims. Nested use of the same lane in one context shares its reservation, and finally releases it on errors. Acquiring a busy lane blocks on a condition without its own timeout; the wrapped operation retains responsibility for cancellation and transport deadlines. Retained local inspect/reconcile reads bypass these remote reservations.

Restart repairs missing records, moves dead attached owners to background observation without relaunch, retains pending attention and spreads overdue checks across 250 ms. The worker holds neither an Agent-turn slot nor parent progression ownership during Gateway I/O. inspect_execution and UI reads remain query-only.

Each actionable fault reason has a versioned incident record. Acknowledged unresolved incidents stay visible but cannot repeatedly wake the model. Verified recovery followed by recurrence can rearm the same reason; repeat_attention_seconds is its minimum recurrence interval. Newly actionable reasons and completion bypass that cooldown. Timestamps, log offsets and different diagnostic commands never create new incidents.
